intent: Find whether adding pairwise feature interaction terms improves held-out AUROC on the synthetic set.

prior_work.reports: Pairwise products of features added to a logistic regression raised AUROC on tabular sets whose labels depend on products of features, and changed nothing on sets whose labels do not.
prior_work.bearing: The nearest work: the same comparison, on real data.

prior_work.reports: A deeper network given no explicit products matched a shallow one given them on its benchmarks.
prior_work.bearing: The competing explanation: a flexible model may find the interaction without the terms.

prior_work.reports: Disagreement between label sources caps the AUROC any model can reach.
prior_work.bearing: Bears only if the labels are noisy beyond their own randomness.

prior_work.reports: A tabular benchmark the owner mentioned.
prior_work.bearing: Would give real data to repeat the comparison on.

feasibility.compute: CPU only, as INTAKE.md states; a logistic regression with or without pairwise products fits on a set of this size in seconds.
feasibility.data: toy/make_synthetic.py writes the synthetic set and split_b is held out, which is enough to answer the question on synthetic data.
feasibility.reasoning: No GPU is needed for the core comparison. The intake does not say which library fits the models, nor how many seeds the generator is run with.

goal_feasibility.reasoning: The generator draws each label from a logistic of a linear term and one product term, so no model can beat the AUROC of the true log-odds, and at the generator's default strengths that ceiling may be close to the 0.85 target. The ceiling cannot be computed without running the generator.

revised_target.why: Below the likely ceiling of the true log-odds at the default strengths, so a model can reach it.

hostile_review: The synthetic set plants the interaction, so recovering it shows only that the method recovers what was put there.
A logistic regression without products is a weak baseline when paper-b reports that a flexible model finds interactions on its own.
One held-out split and one seed give no variance: a gain of 0.01 could be noise.
Trying every pairwise product when one was planted invites reading whichever product helps as a discovery.

directions.title: The comparison as stated
directions.text: Logistic regression with and without pairwise products on the default synthetic set, over several seeds, scored by held-out AUROC on split_b.

directions.title: A flexible second baseline
directions.text: The same comparison, plus a flexible model without products (gradient-boosted trees or a small network), the second baseline paper-b calls for.

directions.title: Where the products stop helping
directions.text: Sweep the generator's interaction strength and find the strength below which the products stop helping.
